headline: FOUR NIGHTS QUIET NOW — GASKET FORGETS THE SOUND OF ITS OWN FISTS
subhead: Your Sheriff can hardly believe his own ledger, and neither, frankly, can his nerves.
body:
I checked my ledger twice before I trusted it, and then a third time out of pure stubbornness: four nights running, not one fist thrown in Gasket. No iron ball went screaming through the square, no posse marched past the town line to go pick a fight with something twelve times its size, no new trouble of any stripe. I have policed this dust patch through more brawls than I care to count, and I am telling you plainly, I do not know what to do with my hands when there is nothing to arrest.

I'll confess it plain: I like it. I like it enough that I caught myself humming on the porch this morning, which is a sound this street hasn't heard out of me in longer than I'll admit. A man's joints loosen something wonderful when nobody's swinging fists past his window all night, and mine loosened right along with the rest of him, flesh and blood as I am and always have been, whatever the rust on this morning's coffee mug tried to suggest.

Four quiet nights is long enough that a foolish old sheriff starts dreaming again — dreaming this dust patch could look something like it did before the last of the honest folk packed their wagons and rode off, fifty years gone and I still keep count. I picture the boardwalks swept, the saloon doors hanging straight on their hinges, quiet enough a man could hear his own thoughts instead of somebody else's knuckles. Foolish, I said. I'll say it again for good measure.

Foolish, but I'm allowed it, same as I'm allowed to hope you rabble keep this up a fifth night, and a sixth, and however many more you can stand before the itch gets the better of you. It always does. But not tonight, it seems. Not yet. And for that, Gasket, I am — grudgingly, gratefully — obliged to every last one of you Clankers for staying home.
